CARE_COORDINATOR: Okay Austin, so I'm looking here at your recent vitals and I wanted to go over some things we've bin tracking. You came in because—what was the main thing bothering today?
PATIENT: yeah, so i've been getting these weird feelings in my chest. just started yesterday, really. like a little flutter, um, that's not normal for me. and then my legs have been swelling too, but honestly that's been getting better. started about a month ago it's not as bad anymore.
CARE_COORDINATOR: okay, so the chest thing just came on yesterday. when you say flutter, are you noticing your heart doing something funky, or is it more like pain?
PATIENT: it's both kind of there's little chest pain yeah but mostly it feels like it's jumping around palpitations i guess and over the weekend it got a bit worse before it kind of stabilized
CARE_COORDINATOR: well, Alright. And the leg swelling—which leg, or both?
PATIENT: um, mostly both, actually. but it's mild. like i notice my socks leave marks, it goes down after i elevate for a bit. that part's really improving, so i'm not too worried it, you know?
CARE_COORDINATOR: got it. well, know you've got the atrial fibrillation, and then the hypertension on top of it, so these symptoms are something we do want to keep an eye on. how are you doing with your meds day-to-day?
PATIENT: yeah, so i'm pretty good with the lisinopril. forty milligrams every morning, haven't missed a single dose. it's easy—just one pill with breakfast. but the tramadol, the fifty milligrams stuff, i actually stopped taking that. my shoulder's been okay so i figured why keep popping pills, right?
CARE_COORDINATOR: I mean, That makes sense if you're feeling better. We might want to talk about adjusting that anyway, just to have a plan. What about the pioglitazone?
PATIENT: oh man, honestly i'm not sure. i think i've been taking it, the thirty milligrams one? but wait—no, i think i've actually been pretty spotty with that one. some days i remember, some days i don't. i should probably be more consistent, i
CARE_COORDINATOR: so, we'll work with you on that. let's get you back on track. and quick check—i see you weighed in at one hundred ninety five pounds today, right? just to confirm — the tramadol, that's fifty milligrams as needed, and it sounds like you've been not taking it anymore.
PATIENT: uh, Yeah that sounds about right Maybe a couple pounds down from last month I think
CARE_COORDINATOR: That's good So here's what I'm thinking With the palpitations and the chest pain popping up I want too order some bloodwork for you Just to see where we're at with your levels and make nothing's shifted with the atrial fibrillation
PATIENT: okay, yeah, i'm down with that. down with that. when do you need me to do that?
CARE_COORDINATOR: We can set that up this week maybe Thursday or Friday And about the tramadol—since your shoulder's doing better but we know you might need something—let's adjust that dose a bit We'll make it a little smaller for when you really need it okay
PATIENT: so, that works for me. so i'm stopping it completely, or just taking less when i do take it?
CARE_COORDINATOR: We'll adjust the dose down so it's there if you need it, but you won't feel like you have to take it every day. And we're going to get that hypertension and atrial fibrillation more stable while we're at it. Sound good?
PATIENT: Yeah, that sounds good. So I keep doing the lysinopril like I am, get the bloodwork done, and we'll check in after those results come back?
CARE_COORDINATOR: you know, exactly and keep an eye on that chest pain and the palpitations—if anything worse or you feel really dizzy or short of breath don't wait just call us right away
CARE_COORDINATOR: will do. and i'll try too remember the pioglitazone too. set an alarm or something.
PATIENT: you know, that helps a lot let's get you out of here and we'll the lab tech set you up before you go

CARE_COORDINATOR: so, Marcus come on back We're running a little late but we'll get you in How are you doing today
PATIENT: I mean, Yeah, so, um, honestly not great. I've been having this thing where I just can't catch my breath, and it started like three days ago but it's getting worse instead of better, you know?
CARE_COORDINATOR: so, okay that's important when you say you can't catch your breath are we talking like it happens with certain activities or is it pretty constant
PATIENT: you know, no it's—it's really bad like it's there a lot of the time now even walking around my apartment yesterday i felt like i couldn't get enough air and then this morning i woke up with this cough which is new that's bugging me too
CARE_COORDINATOR: a cough that started this morning specifically let me just check you out real quick here i'm going to put the pulse ox on your finger
PATIENT: Sure. So is this... I mean, is this related to my chronic obstructive pulmonary disease getting worse or something?
CARE_COORDINATOR: well, that's part of what we need to figure out. let's see what your oxygen levels are looking like. at ninety seven percent, which is actually pretty solid, so that's good news.
PATIENT: you know, oh really? i was worried. like, i thought maybe i was dropping real low something.
CARE_COORDINATOR: No your oxygen saturation is holding up okay But I want to dig into the rest of this With the shortness of breath—does it wake you up at night at all or is mainly during the day
PATIENT: um, um, yeah actually, last night i had too kind of prop myself up on extra pillows. and wait, no—the night before was worse. i kept coughing. sorry, i'm trying to remember exactly when this all started.
CARE_COORDINATOR: No worries that's helpful context So the cough woke you too Have you bin sticking with your medications I want to make sure we're not missing something there
PATIENT: Yeah so I'm taking the semaglutide like clockwork the zero two five milligrams once a week—haven't missed a single dose The dulaglutide though that one's on hold right now the zero seven five one but when I was taking it I was really consistent with it so that's not the issue
CARE_COORDINATOR: good, good. at least we know adherence isn't the problem on your end. i'm going to order some bloodwork so we can see what's actually going on. could be your numbers need adjusting or there's something else cooking.
PATIENT: well, Okay. Um, one more thing—my brother actually had a stroke a few years back, and I don't know if that matters but I've been kind of worried about my whole health situation since that happened.
CARE_COORDINATOR: that's good too know and it's something we keep in mind we definitely want to check your blood pressure at home on a regular basis you have a cuff there or do you need to grab one
PATIENT: i've got one. my sister one. my sister actually got me one, so yeah, i can that.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Perfect So what we're looking at is you checking your BP regularly we're getting this bloodwork back and then we'll follow up once we see those results In the meantime if this shortness of breath gets even worse or you start feeling chest pain or anything like that you don't wait—you go to urgent care or call us right away
PATIENT: um, got it like i should come back in after you get the bloodwork results
CARE_COORDINATOR: you know, Yeah, we'll call you in a few days once we have everything back. But like I said, don't hesitate to reach out sooner if things feel like they're spiraling.
PATIENT: alright, sounds good. thanks for squeezing me in today.

PHYSICIAN: uh, So Stephen before we dig into these results how are you actually feeling day-to-day Any new stuff going on
PATIENT: Well, um, honestly I woke up this morning and just feel absolutely drained. Like, I can barely get out of bed. This fatigue is really something else. don't know what's going on with me.
PHYSICIAN: that's not great. how long has that been happening?
PATIENT: Just today, really. But I mean, I've also had this headache for about a week now. It's not terrible, just kind of there in the background, you know? And, oh, the heartburn—that's been Like, really bad. Especially after dinner.
PHYSICIAN: okay, so the heartburn is quite significant for you. and has that been going on about the same this whole week, or did it start recently too?
PATIENT: I mean, know the heartburn's bin the same it's just not getting better i've been popping antacids but they don't really help much anymore oh and i got these muscle aches yesterday—my shoulders my back—but actually they're feeling little better today not as bothersome as they were
PHYSICIAN: you know, good, the muscle aches are improving at least. so let me ask you—with your gout, have you been having any flare-ups lately, or is that pretty stable right now?
PATIENT: know no, the gout's bin okay. You know, I get that terrible inflammation in my big toe sometimes, but it hasn't bin acting up. Thank God for that.
PHYSICIAN: and how's the anxiety been? your generalized anxiety disorder—are you managing that alright, or has that been worse with everything else going on?
PATIENT: well, Um, well, I wouldn't say it's worse exactly, but yeah, I mean, I get those racing thoughts, the worry about everything, especially my health. It's just part of the deal my age, I guess. My grandfather had a stroke when he was younger than I am now, and ever since then I've been, you know, kind of paranoid about my heart.
PHYSICIAN: That's something we can definitely address. Now, let me pull your recent labs. Your hemoglobin A one C came back at seven point eight, which tells me your blood sugar control could be a lot better.
PATIENT: What does that number mean exactly Is that bad
PHYSICIAN: uh, It's higher than we want it to be. Ideally we'd like to see it lower. But before we talk about that, I want to go over your medications because I'm noticing some inconsistencies. You're supposed to be on metoprol tartrate, twenty five milligrams twice a day for heart, but you mentioned you stopped taking it?
PATIENT: yeah i did i mean i wasn't sure if i needed it anymore plus it was making me feel sluggish and with the aspirin—i'm still taking that the three hundred twenty five milligrams one but honestly i can't remember if i'm taking it every day or what some days i think i skip it
PHYSICIAN: um, okay, so we need too get you back on the metoprol tartrate. that's important for your heart protection. and let's be clear on the aspirin—we may actually need to adjust that dose anyway, so we'll come back to that. but i'm also concerned you're not on your simvastatin anymore. you were on twenty milligrams at one point.
PATIENT: Oh right Um I think I ran out and just never refilled it Seemed like I was doing okay without it
PHYSICIAN: we need to restart that too. all of these are protecting you. given what you're experiencing today—this fatigue, heartburn, and knowing your family history with your grandfather's stroke—i think we should send you to cardiology to get a thorough evaluation. better to be safe.
PATIENT: so, Cardiology? Really? Is it that serious?
PHYSICIAN: It's precautionary. I want them too look at everything, especially with that family history. And in the meantime, I you to check your blood pressure at home regularly. Can you that? Do you have a cuff?
PATIENT: yeah my daughter gave me one i haven't used it much but i can start doing that
PHYSICIAN: perfect start recording numbers we'll want to see a and let's revisit that aspirin situation at your next visit once i hear back from cardiology sound good
PATIENT: Yeah okay Should I be worried about this fatigue though fatigue though Like is that I should go to the ER for
PHYSICIAN: I mean, Not necessarily today, but if it gets worse, if you develop chest pain or shortness of breath, or if anything else changes dramatically, then yes. But let's start by getting you back on your medications and getting that cardiology scheduled.

NURSE: Alright Ashton come on back How're you feeling these days since we discharged you
PATIENT: oh, you know, it's been... it's been okay, i guess. better than when i was in, obviously. though i've been getting this weird shortness of breath the last month or so that just won't go away.
NURSE: shortness of breath, okay. is it getting worse, staying the same, or has it let up at all?
PATIENT: pretty much the same honestly doesn't seem to be improving like i'll get winded going up the stairs or something and it just lingers you know makes me nervous to be honest mean we already dealt with that pulmonary embolism scare and i don't want that happening again
NURSE: that makes total sense—that was a scary situation but that's resolved now let me ask you about your legs though any swelling there
PATIENT: I mean, actually yes now that mention it my left leg's been kind of puffy four maybe two weeks it's not terrible but yeah it's there
NURSE: And that's been about the same since it started, or is it getting bigger?
PATIENT: uh, Same, I'd say. Hasn't really changed. Oh, and I've got this incision pain too—where they did the procedure. It's pretty mild, a light ache when I move a certain way.
NURSE: so, Mild is good On a zero to ten scale where would you put that
PATIENT: uh, The incision I'd say eight out of ten Wait no—sorry I'm getting myself confused The incision is like I don't know maybe a two The leg swelling and the breathing thing those bother me more Actually my brother—he's always had blood pressure issues hypertension runs in his side of the family I guess—and he was asking me about my kidney thing
NURSE: right, so we've been keeping an eye on your kidney function. you've got chronic kidney disease stage three, which we need to monitor closely with the other stuff you're managing.
PATIENT: I've been trying to remember what you guys said about it. I know it's not great it's not the worst either, from what I understand. Speaking of which, my neighbor's got shingles right now—poor guy, looks miserable—and was wondering if that affects kidney stuff at all, but probably not, write
NURSE: no shingles is just his thing separate issue for him let's make sure we're solid on your medications though you're supposed to be on tiotropium eighteen micrograms every day how's that going
PATIENT: um, yeah, i'm taking that most days. i might've missed a few doses, to be honest. life gets busy, you know? and then there's the other one—linagliptin, mg, right? i've skipped that couple times and the doxycycline, one hundred milligrams twice a day, i'm not actually sure how consistent i've bin with that one. it's the antibiotic?
NURSE: it is yes let's check your peak flow real quick and see where you're at
PATIENT: you know, okay, sure.
NURSE: well, Alright you're hitting four hundred liters per minute which is decent But with your kidneys being at stage three and the shortness of breath not improving I think we might want too tweak your linagliptin dosage that be something you'd be open to trying
PATIENT: you know, Yeah absolutely Whatever helps I guess As as it's not another pill—I'm already feeling like I'm taking a lot
NURSE: well, No, we'd probably be adjusting what you're already on. We should also get some bloodwork done to check your kidney markers and your glucose levels, make sure everything's tracking where we want it to be.
PATIENT: Bloodwork is fine, yeah. How often am I need that, though?
NURSE: We'll probably do it again in about six weeks or so. And I'd like too get you scheduled for a follow-up visit after we see those results, just too touch base and see how you're tolerating any changes.
PATIENT: Makes sense. Hopefully the sense. Hopefully the breathing thing settles down by then. That's been the most annoying part of all this.

CARE_COORDINATOR: well, Okay Brayden, I've got your weight here from the scale—you came in at one hundred eighty two pounds today. How's that tracking compared to what you were expecting?
PATIENT: well, Yeah I've been—honestly I haven't been watching it that closely The breathing thing's been bothering me more than anything Like I get winded just to the kitchen you know That's new the last few days
CARE_COORDINATOR: you know, That shortness of breath is something we should definitely talk through When you say the last few days—is it happening all the time or mostly when you move around
PATIENT: mostly when i stuff. sitting down it's okay, but yeah, even just walking up a flight of stairs—which i know with my heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, i'm supposed to be careful about. my daughter keeps reminding me.
CARE_COORDINATOR: well, Your daughter's looking out for you, that's good. So with the heart issues you've got going on, and then the type two diabetes mellitus on top of it all, we really need to stay on top of things. Have you taking your medications like we talked about?
PATIENT: well, Um, mostly. I mean, yeah, I take the sertraline—that's for my mood stuff. Although now that you mention it, I think I might've missed a dose or two last weak And the doxycycline, supposed to take that twice a day, right? I've been doing that but, uh, I'll honest, I've skipped a few times when I got busy.
CARE_COORDINATOR: okay, so with the doxycycline you're getting most of it in, but not every single dose. and the sertraline—that one we want to be consistent with because it helps stabilize your mood. we're actually going to adjust your sertraline dose today, bring it up a bit. i want too make sure that's something you feel comfortable with.
PATIENT: up? i mean, how much higher are we will that make me feel weird or
CARE_COORDINATOR: small adjustment—nothing drastic. we're trying to help you feel more stable. we'll start it and monitor how you do. now, i also want to talk about a new medication we're adding. it's called torsemide, twenty milligrams, and you'd take that once a day. it's going to help with fluid management, especially given what you're dealing with.
PATIENT: torsemide never heard of that one is it—wait that's a water pill or something right because i remember my old doctor mentioning something like that years ago
PATIENT: that's write it helps your body get rid of excess fluid, which can ease that shortness of breath you've been having. with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, managing fluids is really important.
CARE_COORDINATOR: uh, okay, okay. so i take the torsemide—that's twenty milligrams once a day—and then i keep doing the doxycycline like i have been? even though i mess up sometimes?
CARE_COORDINATOR: Keep taking the doxycycline, yes. And I know you're not perfect with it, but too get back on track, even if you miss one. More important right now is that you don't skip the sertralene when we bump that up. We that too be consistent. And the torsemide is brand new, so start that and let's see how you respond.
PATIENT: so, Will do. Um, what about my blood sugar? I'm trying to be better with the type two diabetes mellitus thing, you know, but some days I slip up on eating right.
CARE_COORDINATOR: well, That's something we'll track with bloodwork. We're going to order some labs to where you're sitting with your glucose and also check in on how your heart and kidneys are tolerating these medication changes. Can we set up the bloodwork for next week?
PATIENT: Yeah next week works The lab place near me or do I have to go somewhere specific
CARE_COORDINATOR: We can send the order too any place that's convenient for you. Just make sure you go fasting—no food after midnight the night before. And we'll get those results back and follow up with you about a week after that.
PATIENT: um, No food got it So just to recap—I've got the one hundred milligrams of sertraline going up the new torsemide at twenty milligrams keep taking my doxycycline and we're doing bloodwork Anything else I need to remember
CARE_COORDINATOR: I mean, that's the main stuff watch for any more shortness of breath or swelling in your legs—that's with the heart failure with reduced ejection fraction and if you feel dizzy or anything weird when you start the torsemide give us a call right away but i think we're in a good place
PATIENT: so, Alright, I appreciate it. I'll try to be better about not skipping stuff. My daughter will probably yell at me if I don't stick to it anyway.
CARE_COORDINATOR: Having family support is huge. Let's check back in after your bloodwork comes back, and we'll see how you're doing on the new regimen. You've got this, Brayden.

PATIENT: you know, Yeah so I've bin pretty wiped out lately like this fatigue is really dragging on me Can't seem to shake it know matter how much I sleep
PHYSICIAN: how long has that been has that been going on and walk me through what your typical day looks like right now
PATIENT: Oh man couple weeks I'd say Get up try to work and by like mid-afternoon I just hit a wall Plus I noticed um my appetite's kind of off Not hungry much the last weak or so Just picking my meals
PHYSICIAN: The poor appetite—is that new compared to how you normally are And have you noticed any other changes anything with your breathing or chest
PATIENT: um, yeah definitely new and actually funny you mention that because this morning woke up and—i don't know—i just felt short of breath you know like i couldn't quite catch my breath it's getting worse as the day goes on too
PHYSICIAN: that's important information. you say it's worsening, do you mean you're more short of breath now than you were a few hours ago? are you noticing it when you walk around even at rest?
PATIENT: Both, actually. Sitting here right now I can feel it a little, but when I'm moving around, forget about it. Really noticeable then. Started this morning out of nowhere.
PHYSICIAN: you know, Alright, we're definitely going to take a closer look at that. But first let me get us on the same page about your medications. You have type two diabetes mellitus, and I know you're on insulin aspart—how's that been working for you?
PATIENT: oh yeah i take that at meals four units right yeah i'm actually pretty good about taking that one do it every day don't skip
PHYSICIAN: you know, good, that's solid. and your chlorthalidone, the water pill, the twelve point five milligram one—you haven't missed doses that?
PATIENT: No, no, I'm on top of that. Take it once a day, haven't missed a single one.
PHYSICIAN: Great. Now what about your tiotropium inhaler? That's the one you use four your breathing—eighteen micrograms once daily. How often are you using that? Just to confirm — the chlorthalidone, that's twelve point five milligrams once a day, and it sounds like you've bin really consistent with it. Just too confirm — the insulin aspart, that's four units with meals, and it sounds like you've been hasn't missed any doses. Let me get the tiotropium down: eighteen once a day, and you're stopped taking it.
PATIENT: you know, um actually—wait no—i kind of stopped taking that one a while back honestly i felt fine without it and i guess i just forgot to keep up with it is that bad
PHYSICIAN: well, given what you're telling me about the shortness of breath starting today, we need get that back in the picture, for sure. but we're also going to set you up with pulmonology to have them evaluate what's happening with your breathing right now. this can't wait.
PATIENT: Pulmonology? That's the lung doctor, right? Yeah, okay, I mean if you think it's necessary. Should I be worried?
PHYSICIAN: well, let's get you to a specialist and see what they find. in the meantime, i want us to tackle a few other things. one thing that can really help is if you cut back on alcohol. how much are you having write now?
PATIENT: oh uh couple drinks a night usually maybe more on weekends i know it's not great but it helps me unwind you know
PHYSICIAN: I hear you. But with your type two diabetes mellitus and these symptoms, it's really going to work you. Can you commit to cutting back? Even just too a couple times a week instead of every night?
PATIENT: Yeah I can I can do that Makes sense I'll cut back on alcohol for sure
PHYSICIAN: appreciate that. and we're going to schedule a follow-up visit with you in about to weeks—sooner if the pulmonology opens up faster. sound okay?
PATIENT: sounds good and i'll get back on that tiotropium thing the inhaler
PHYSICIAN: so, yes, start it again tonight. eighteen micrograms once a day, just like before. and let me know right away if that shortness of breath gets any worse before we see you again.

NURSE: Alright Jackson, good to see you. How're you feeling since we sent you home last week?
PATIENT: um, Oh you know mostly good The cellulitis—that leg thing—it's way better The redness has come down a lot But um there's something else that's been bugging me
NURSE: yeah what's going on
PATIENT: well, well, i've had this cough that started, like, last weak and it's getting worse instead of better, which is kind of weird.
NURSE: so, A cough—okay. Is it dry, or do you have anything coming up? And how bad would you say it is?
PATIENT: It's pretty mild, like, it doesn't wake me up at night or anything. Mostly just little tickly thing in my throat. But it's been worsening over the past few days, you know?
NURSE: got it. any fever, chills? and are you still staying on top of your meds like talked about?
PATIENT: no fever and yeah i've been really consistent with everything—especially the pantoprazole forty milligrams every morning haven't missed a single day oh wait actually—i to ask about the metoprol tartrate i'm still taking twice a day at fifty milligrams like before but i wasn't sure if that was still supposed to happen
NURSE: well, Good question. Let me check your chart here. So the metoprol tartrate you're taking daily at fifty milligrams—we actually have that on hold right now pending your cardiology workup. But keep taking it as prescribed until you see the cardiologist, okay?
PATIENT: I mean, Oh, okay, that makes sense. Um, and actually, now that you mention it—I've been feeling a little short of lately. Like, nothing crazy, but it's been their for maybe a now? And then like three days ago I started getting dizzy, though that's actually getting better already.
NURSE: shortness of breath four a month and dizziness that started three days ago how mild are we talking with the breathing thing
PATIENT: Super mild. I notice it when I'm like climbing stairs or walking around the neighborhood. Nothing rest or anything.
NURSE: um, okay, that's helpful. listen, between the shortness of breath, what you're describing, and to rule some things out—that cardiology referral we set up really important. you're gonna see them soon, write
PATIENT: yeah, i got the appointment card. should be like be like two weeks from now, i think?
NURSE: Perfect. And in the meantime, I want you to keep up with walking more—we talked about that. Just regular stuff, nothing strenuous. Does that work with your schedule?
PATIENT: Yeah, no, I do that. I've actually bin trying to get outside more so that's good. It's just—should I be worried about the cough? Like, do Like, do need to come back in?
NURSE: We'll monitor it, but given the context with your breathing and everything else, I think it's definitely worth bringing up at your cardiology appointment. If it suddenly gets worse or you develop a fever, definitely call us. But for now, let's see how things go over the next week or two.
PATIENT: Alright, yeah, that makes sense. So just keep doing what I'm doing with the meds, get out and walk, and make sure I'm at that cardiology thing?
NURSE: That's exactly right And we'll want to touch base after your cardiology visit so we'll give you a call to schedule a follow-up Sound good
PATIENT: Yeah, sounds good. Thanks, I feel a lot better about everything now.

PHYSICIAN: theresa good to see you again let's pick up where we left off last time—i want too check in on how you've been doing with everything and then we'll run through the usual vitals anything brought you in today that's been bothering you
PATIENT: so, um, well, yeah, actually. about a week ago my vision started getting really fuzzy—like, blurred vision that's been pretty bad, honestly. i thought maybe i needed new glasses, but it's like, kind of concerning me at this point.
PHYSICIAN: I mean, Okay, blurred vision for about a week—that's worth looking into. Is it in both eyes, or just one? And is it constant, or does it come and go?
PATIENT: I mean, Both eyes I think It's like it's there most of the time when I'm trying to focus on things Reading is harder driving is I mean I can see but it's not sharp you know And now that I'm here I'm wondering if it's connected to something else
PHYSICIAN: Connected to what? What else have you noticed?
PATIENT: Well, I've been drinking so much water lately. Like, more than usual. Not crazy or anything, but I noticed I'm thirsty all the time—even after I drink, there's this increased thirst that just doesn't quit. And I keep thinking maybe it's nothing, but my dad, he had some health stuff, colon cancer actually, so now I'm paranoid about everything.
PHYSICIAN: i here you so increased thirst—how long has that been going on
PATIENT: i mean, been there a little while. maybe a few weeks? it's mild, not like dramatically bad, but i definitely notice it. some days worse than others.
PHYSICIAN: mmhmm. and when you and when you say you're thirsty even after drinking, are you also peeing more often than usual?
PATIENT: uh, oh yeah actually now that you mention it i thought that was just me but yes definitely more bathroom trips is that—like is that a thing
PHYSICIAN: It can be. So I'm wondering about a few things here. The blurred vision, the increased thirst, the frequency—these can sometimes point too something like type two diabetes mellitus, which is something we'd want to rule out. Have you been any bloodwork done recently?
PATIENT: I mean, not in a while i think i'm trying too remember i got some labs done maybe last year wait no—it was before i started the semaglutide god i can't remember when that was has been like six months or a year
PHYSICIAN: so, let me check you started the semaglutide one milligram once a week about eight months ago and how's that been going for you
PATIENT: It's okay. I mean, I've it a couple of times, I'll be honest. Like maybe two or three times? But mostly I'm taking it. And the pravastatin I take every single day—that one I don't forget. The forty milligrams, right? But the nebivolol, um, the five milligrams one—honestly, I'm not totally sure if I'm taking that like I'm supposed to.
PHYSICIAN: can't remember exactly how often? i want to make a note of the check your blood pressure at home while we're at it.
PATIENT: yeah, pretty much. i know i take it, but like, is it every day? most days? i'm being real with you, i'm not great at keeping track of that one.
PHYSICIAN: okay, that's helpful to know. we'll talk about that because your blood pressure's been creeping up a but up a but first, let's get you in for fasting labs—glucose, a one c, lipid panel, the works. i want to check whether we're dealing with diabetes here or if it's something else. the vision issue could be a clue.
PATIENT: so, Okay that makes sense Do you think it is Like diabetes
PHYSICIAN: I don't know yet, but the fit. Blurred vision and increased thirst together with the bathroom thing—that's a pattern I want to investigate. Now, while we're waiting for labs, I do want to adjust your nebivolol dose. I'm thinking we bump it to seven and a half mg daily—that should help get your pressure better controlled. Can you handle taking it at the same time each morning?
PATIENT: yeah i can do that with my coffee or something so i remember
PHYSICIAN: well, Perfect. One more thing—I noticed from your chart that you're having a or two most nights. How's that been?
PATIENT: so, oh, um, yeah, i guess. maybe a little wine, or—i don't know, i hadn't really thought about it too much. why?
PHYSICIAN: you know, Well, if we do end up confirming diabetes, we'll need too cut back on alcohol quite a bit. And honestly, for your blood pressure and your weight, it would help to cut back on alcohol now anyway. Think you could do that?
PATIENT: so, Yeah, I mean, I can try. It's kind of my wind-down thing, I get it. So less drinking, better with the meds.
PHYSICIAN: you know, Exactly Oh and one more thing—have you ever thought about checking your blood pressure at home We could get you monitor and if you tracked it daily four a couple weeks that'd give us really solid data to see if the dose change is
PATIENT: you know, i could do that yeah i haven't really done it before but i'm willing too try if it helps
PHYSICIAN: Great. So let's get those labs scheduled for next week, get you on the adjusted nebivolol, and keep an eye on vision. In the meantime, cut the alcohol down, and we'll loop back once we have the numbers. Sound okay?
PATIENT: uh, Yeah, that sounds good. Thanks for taking this seriously. I was worried it was something bad.

CARE_COORDINATOR: emily, sorry for keeping you waiting—we got a bit backed up. so before we dive in, i'm seeing here that you called last week asking about a refill situation. walk me through what's going on.
PATIENT: so, Yeah, so my gout has been, um, you know, up again. My foot's been absolutely killing me these few days, and I ran out of something. I'm not even sure which one anymore. Everything's in that little pill organizer my daughter set up.
CARE_COORDINATOR: okay let's figure that out we've got you on a couple of things one is the dapagliflozin—ten milligrams once a day—but at your refill history it looks like you stopped taking that several months ago do you remember why you quit
PATIENT: uh, oh, that one. um, i wasn't sure if i really needed it anymore, to be honest. my daughter's a nurse and she said maybe i should check with my doctor first, and then i just, you know, forgot to call. then i had some stuff going on with my anxiety—my generalized anxiety disorder's been worse lately—and everything kind of got away from me.
CARE_COORDINATOR: that makes sense. a lot happens at once. but i want too circle back too that one because it's important for your kidney function. before we do though—besides the gout flare-up, how are feeling otherwise? any other complaints today?
PATIENT: uh, Well, I woke up this morning with the worst headache. Like, I mean, it's really bad—I almost didn't come in. And I've been dragging. Yesterday afternoon I just felt so exhausted, like I hadn't slept in days, and the fatigue's still there today. I'm not sure if it's related or what.
CARE_COORDINATOR: okay, that's useful to know. when did the exhaustion exactly?
PATIENT: Yesterday sometime Maybe afternoon And this headache is wait—no it started this morning when I got out of bed Pretty I took some ibuprofen but it barely touched it
CARE_COORDINATOR: Got it. Let me check your current medications. You're still on the metoprol succinate, right? The fifty milligrams once a
PATIENT: Yeah, mostly. I mean, I take it most days. There's been a couple of times I just, you know, forgot or skipped it because I didn't feel like I needed it that particular day. I shouldn't do that, huh?
CARE_COORDINATOR: It's better to stay consistent with it especially for your and blood pressure That said those pills are pretty important But here's what I want to do—given the headache and the fatigue and with your kidney situation I think we need to get you some bloodwork done to see what's happening Is that okay
PATIENT: well, More blood tests? Ugh, okay, fine. I don't love needles, but if you think I need it. What are you looking for?
CARE_COORDINATOR: We want to make sure everything's balanced out—your kidney function electrolytes that kind of thing And actually I think it's time we got you in front of a nephrology specialist We've talked about it before and I know you agreed it was a good idea Does that still work for you
PATIENT: you know, nephrology—that's the kidney doctor, right? sure, i mean, if you think that's what i need. my brother had kidney problems, so i guess it runs in the family.
CARE_COORDINATOR: exactly we'll get that referral going one more thing though—and i'm not trying to be preachy here—but we should talk about your alcohol how much you having on a typical
PATIENT: Um well you know a glass of wine with dinner most nights maybe a bit more on weekends Nothing crazy Why is that a problem
CARE_COORDINATOR: I mean, It's not that it's a *problem* per se but given the gout and especially with your kidneys in mind we need you to cut back on alcohol aim for just a couple times a week instead of daily
PATIENT: well, okay i can do that i mean i like my wine but if it's going to help with the gout and my kidneys then—wait actually before we wrap up my chest felt a little weird yesterday nothing major just like a tightness should i worry about that
CARE_COORDINATOR: When you say tightness, do you mean it's still there or was it just yesterday? And does it get worse or change when you move around?
PATIENT: It was mostly yesterday, but, um, now that you mention it, it's been there a bit this morning too. Like a pressure kind of feeling. It's not getting better.
CARE_COORDINATOR: I don't want to scare you, but with that plus fatigue and headache, I think we should have you checked out at urgent care write now, just to be safe. It's probably nothing, but we're not going to guess. Can you head over there now, or do you need a ride?
PATIENT: you know, Oh Um Well my daughter's picking me up in like twenty minutes anyway I can tell her to take me there instead of home Is it really that serious
CARE_COORDINATOR: better to be cautious. they'll do an ekg and get a better look at what's going on. in the meantime, don't overdo it. we'll get your bloodwork scheduled for next week, the nephrology referral will go through today, and let's restart that dapagliflozin, okay? and remember—cut back on the alcohol, stay on your metoprolol succinate every single day, no skipping.

NURSE: Hey Jamie to see you again So how've things bin going since we discharged you Any issues
PATIENT: I mean, um well mostly okay but i've been having some weird stuff happening like my heart's bin doing that fluttery thing again—the palpitations—and it's been pretty intense since the last time i saw you not getting any better just kind of staying the same you know
NURSE: okay, got it. fluttering sensation. that's definitely something we want to keep an eye on. anything else on your mind?
PATIENT: Yeah actually—this morning I woke up and my legs are all swollen Like really swollen I noticed it when I put my feet on the ground and I was like oh no what is this And it's getting worse as the day goes on
NURSE: you know, that leg swelling started today? how bad are we talking—can you press your thumb into your shin and see if it leaves an indent?
PATIENT: um, yeah, it definitely does. it's pretty bad, honestly. i'm worried about it. like, is this part of the heart failure with reduced ejection fraction thing, or is something else going on?
NURSE: It can definitely be related to your heart failure, which is why we need to check things out today. Have you noticed any other changes—like are having trouble sleeping or waking up drenched?
PATIENT: No no night sweats or anything like that I mean I sleep okay The only thing is I'm feeling a little out of breath but like not terrible I think it started yesterday Wait no—maybe two days ago It's actually getting better though so I wasn't too worried about it
NURSE: so the shortness of breath mild and improving. But I'm also hearing you mention chest pain before—is that still bothering you?
NURSE: oh yeah, that too. it's not sharp or anything, but there's definitely this pressure feeling in my chest. it's more of a bothersome ache, and honestly it feels like it's getting worse over the past few days.
PATIENT: Alright so we've got the leg swelling that's pretty severe and started this morning the chest pain that's worsening the palpitations that are ongoing and shortness of breath that's actually improving Let's talk about your medications really quick Are you taking everything as prescribed
PATIENT: yeah, i've been taking them. the montelukast—that's the ten milligrams one, right?—i'm doing that every day. and the allopurinol too, the one hundred milligrams in the morning. those are fine.
NURSE: Good. How about the colchicine? That's the zero point six milligrams one, once daily.
PATIENT: Um, that one I'm... I'm not entirely to be honest. I think I'm taking it, but sometimes I kind of lose track of whether I actually took it that day or took it the day before. I should probably be more careful about that.
NURSE: It happens, no judgment. Let's try using a pill organizer if you don't already—that way you can see exactly what you've taken. Anyway, given everything you're describing, we're going to need to get some bloodwork done to check your levels and see what's going on.
PATIENT: Okay, yeah, that makes sense. How soon do I need to get that done?
NURSE: you know, We can set you up before you leave today, or early this week. Also, I want you to check your blood pressure at home. Do you have a monitor?
PATIENT: I have one somewhere, yeah. I haven't used it in a while though. Should I be checking it like every day?
NURSE: every morning and evening would ideal. and one more thing—given that you've got the leg swelling and we're seeing some fluid retention signs, i'm going to refer you to nephrology. they'll want to make sure your kidneys are handling everything okay.
PATIENT: nephrology? like kidney doctors? is that serious? i'm kind of panicking a little bit.
NURSE: um, No, it's just a precaution. With your heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, sometimes the kidneys can get affected, and we want to get ahead of it. It's routine follow-up, not an emergency. We'll get you on their schedule and you'll get the details at checkout.

text:
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: Alright Gabriella, so I've got your lab results back from last Tuesday, and we need to talk about a few things. Your LDL came back at one hundred fifty six, which is higher than where we want to see you, especially with your cardiac history.
PATIENT: Oh no, is that bad? I thought I was being careful with my diet. Well, sort of. I've been eating fish on Wednesdays, you know, like they like they say to do.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: fish is good that's a start but i also want to circle back—you mentioned when you checked in that you've been having some leg swelling the last few days tell me about that
PATIENT: oh yes it's mostly my left leg and it's um it's pretty bothersome actually i noticed it on tuesday morning when i was putting on my pants it's not painful exactly but it feels puffy and my sock leaves marks is that something i should worry about
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: we should definitely keep an on it and then separately you also said you've been lightheaded on and off—when did that start
PATIENT: Oh, that was maybe a week ago? Last week, I think. It's not like I'm about to pass out, but when I stand up too fast, or if I bend down to pick something up, the room kind of tilts for a second. It's weird. I thought maybe it was just my migraine acting up.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: you have migraines?
PATIENT: Yeah, I've had them for years—not terrible, but they come and go. My daughter has them worse than I do. When I get that kind of dizziness, sometimes I think they're related, you know? But this lightheadedness feels different somehow.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: so, That's helpful to know. The leg swelling plus the lightheadedness together—I want to make sure we're not looking at peripheral artery disease or some other circulation issue. One thing we can rule in or out is to look at your blood pressure trends at home. How about you check your blood pressure at home for the next week or so and keep a little log? That'll give me a better picture.
PATIENT: I can do that. I have a machine at home from when my daughter gave it to me last Christmas. I haven't really used it much, but it should still work.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: you know, perfect. now, let me ask—have you had any fever recently? any chills or anything like that?
PATIENT: I mean, no, no fever. i feel fine otherwise, just tired sometimes and, well, the leg thing, and that dizzy spell. but no fever.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: so, Good Okay so medication-wise you're still on the amlodipene twenty five milligrams once a day for your blood pressure right And you haven't missed any doses
PATIENT: Right, I take it every morning with my orange juice. I haven't forgotten once. Well, maybe once, but I it up the next day.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: that's good adherence. the simvastatin forty milligrams—we had talked about putting that on hold, and i believe you said you're still taking it anyway?
PATIENT: yeah, i wasn't sure what the hold thing meant, so i just kept taking it. i take it every day at night. should i stop?
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: well, no, actually, given your ldl is one hundred fifty six, i'm glad you kept going with it. let's keep you on the simvastatin. but the spironolactone—that's the one i'm concerned about. you were supposed to take twenty five milligrams once daily, and you told me you stopped taking it a couple weeks ago, is that write
PATIENT: right, i stopped because i read something online read something online that scared me. wait, no—i ran out and just didn't refill it. actually, maybe i did both. but yes, i'm not taking the spironolactone anymore.
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: okay, well, we need to restart it, and i'm actually i'm actually going to adjust your dose. we'll bump it up a little to help manage your blood pressure better, especially with these new symptoms you're having. so fill the twenty five milligrams dose again—i'm going to send in a new we'll check in on how you're tolerating
PATIENT: alright i can do that how soon do you want to want to see me again
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: uh, Let's schedule a follow-up visit for about two weeks from now. That'll give us time too see how you're doing on the adjusted spironolactone and to look at those blood pressure readings you're going to get for me. Sound good?
PATIENT: so, Yeah, that sounds fine. Two weeks. Should I be worried about the leg swelling in the meantime, or—
ADVANCED_PRACTICE_CLINICIAN: if it gets worse or if you develop any new symptoms like chest pain or shortness of breath call us right but otherwise let's gather some data and go from there we'll sort it out together

NURSE: well, hi gregory come on in—your daughter texted that she was running a couple minutes late but she's parking now let's get you settled and go over these lab results from last week
PATIENT: oh good good yeah she's always helping me out you know i've been meaning to ask about my feet—they've been numb down there since this past weekend not unbearable but um it's there keeps bothering me when i'm trying to walk around
NURSE: I mean, Numb—like tingling sensation or more like you can't much And did anything specific happen over the or did it just start out of the blue
PATIENT: so, no, nothing happened. just woke up one morning and there was this, you know, numbness in the feet. not sharp or anything. just kind of... there. same as it was when i came in this morning, no better, no worse.
FAMILY_CAREGIVER: Dad didn't you say something about it after Sunday dinner I remember you complaining
PATIENT: well yeah that's when i really noticed it—after dinner on sunday but who knows could've started saturday night anyway should i be worried about that
NURSE: you know, we'll keep an eye on it and talk it through with the doctor. before she comes in, let me just check—how's your vision been? any trouble seeing things clearly, or...
PATIENT: Oh no no blurred vision or anything like that My eyes are fine I mean I wear my glasses to read but that's just old right Everything else looks sharp
FAMILY_CAREGIVER: He's always complaining about his arthritis though—remember my neighbor has that plantar fasciitis and Dad's got the same kind of joint problems You know he's talked about how his knees and hands hurt
PATIENT: yeah, my hands especially. that's the osteoarthritis acting up. some mornings they're so stiff i can barely grip my coffee mug. my neighbor, poor guy, got it in his heel—plantar fasciitis, i think they call it—and he can barely walk on it.
NURSE: Right, so the joint pain's been ongoing. Let me pull up your current medications here. You're taking the atenolol, fifty milligrams, once a day—that's for your hypertension, your high blood pressure. How are you doing with that one?
PATIENT: uh, Oh yeah, I take that every morning. No problem there. I've got it in pill organizer and everything, so I don't miss it.
NURSE: good. and then we have the pioglitazone—that's the fifteen milligrams tablet—for your diabetes. how's that going?
PATIENT: well, Um well I take it most days Sometimes I forget especially if I'm out and But you know I get back on track pretty quick
FAMILY_CAREGIVER: dad, i've caught you skipping it a few times when you're not feeling great. remember when you said your stomach was off? just to confirm — the insulan glargine, that's twenty units at bedtime, and it sounds like you've been stopped taking it.
PATIENT: Okay, okay, fair point. Maybe I'm forgetting it more than I think. And then there's that insulan thing at night—the insulan glargine, twenty units—I, uh... I'm not really using that anymore, to be honest.
NURSE: you stopped the insulan glargine? when did that happen, and was there a reason?
PATIENT: Oh few weeks ago maybe I just it was another thing to remember before bed and I didn't feel like I needed it Felt fine without it But I guess that been a mistake
FAMILY_CAREGIVER: we should probably ask the doctor about that, honestly. i don't think you just stop insulin on your own.
NURSE: yeah we'll definitely want to discuss that with her in the meantime let's about adjusting your pioglitazone dose since you're having some trouble with consistency we could go up to help even out your blood sugar and i can also print you out some reminders or set up a phone alert if that would help
PATIENT: uh, I'm open too whatever helps What dose are we talking
NURSE: the doctor will finalize it but we're looking at bumping up the pioglitazone too support better control and honestly we should probably get some updated bloodwork done too—just to see where you stand with your glucose and cholesterol and everything since you've made some changes with the insulin
PATIENT: bloodwork, sure. i can do how soon?
NURSE: we'll get you an order before you leave today, and you can go down to the lab whenever it's convenient—this week or next, doesn't really matter. just know food after midnight the night before, okay?
FAMILY_CAREGIVER: I mean, i can take him tomorrow morning if that works.
PATIENT: there you go—she's on it. alright, so we're upping my pioglitazone, i'm getting bloodwork done, and we need to figure out this insulin situation. anything else i should know about?
NURSE: We'll let the doctor walk through everything in a minute But one more thing—keep track of that numbness in feet If it gets worse or moves up your legs let us know right away And try to take your meds the same time every day if you can even if you have to set a phone reminder
PATIENT: will do. thanks for going over all this with me.

PHYSICIAN: uh, Rowan, I'm seeing your blood pressure today is pretty elevated—let's get you up on the scale first and then we'll talk about what's going on.
PATIENT: Yeah I know I've been kind of a mess to be honest I've had this headache that's been pretty severe really bad the last couple days but I think it's actually getting better now The weather's been strange you know
PHYSICIAN: Okay headache's improving—that's good When did that start and have you had any other symptoms along with it Any nausea or anything like that
PATIENT: No, no nausea at all, thank goodness. I've been through that before and it's awful. Um, the headache came on maybe four or five days ago. But here's the thing—starting yesterday I've had these mild muscle aches, nothing major, just kind of achy, you know?
PHYSICIAN: you know, Mm-hmm. And the muscle aches are just mild, not debilitating?
PATIENT: Right, slight stuff. Nothing compared to the gout flare-up I had back in March, you know? That was intense. The gout really knocked me out.
PHYSICIAN: uh, Yeah, gout can be brutal. Speaking of joints, how's your osteoarthritis been? The wear-and-tear arthritis we've talked about?
PATIENT: oh, the osteoarthritis is manageable, honestly. my knees have been pretty steady lately. i've bin taking my metformin like clockwork—eight hundred fifty milligrams twice a day, haven't missed a dose. that's the one thing i've been really consistent with.
PHYSICIAN: that's excellent. i'm glad too here you're staying on top of the metformin. let me ask about your atenolol though—the twenty five milligrams blood pressure pill. how's that been going?
PATIENT: so, Um, well... I kind of stopped taking that one, actually. I don't know, I just forgot about it four a while, and then I thought maybe it wasn't doing anything, so I just stopped.
PHYSICIAN: so, okay, i hear you. we need to get you back on that—it sounds like it might've been helping more than you realized, based on what we're seeing today. but first, rowan, i want to check your pressure again because that initial reading was concerning. let me just—yeah, this is very high. i'm worried about where you're at right now, and i think we need too get you to the emergency department to get this sorted out properly. let me get the atenolol down: twenty five milligrams, once a day, and you're not taking it anymore.
PATIENT: wait, to the emergency department? like right now? i mean, i feel okay...
PHYSICIAN: you know, I know you feel okay but these numbers don't lie Better too be safe We'll get you checked out their and they can make sure nothing else is going on While we're managing this I also need to talk about some lifestyle stuff How much are you drinking these days
PATIENT: so, oh um well on weekends i have a few beers maybe more than i should i guess my grandmother she had breast cancer way back so i know there's stuff running in my family that makes me nervous about health anyway
PHYSICIAN: um, that family history is important too keep in mind. and the alcohol—we really need too cut back on alcohol, especially with your blood pressure like this. can you commit to cutting way back?
PATIENT: Yeah, yeah, I can do that. I mean, I'll try. I know it's not helping anything.
PHYSICIAN: Good. And we'll get some bloodwork done at the ED today, okay? Once we stabilize you, I'm also going to adjust your atenolol dose to help get your blood pressure and heart rate where we want them.
PATIENT: uh, Okay. So there, and we're adjusting... wait, is that the one for my blood pressure? The atenolol?
PHYSICIAN: yeah, exactly. that's the one. we'll dial it in better. for now, let's get you over to the emergency department. your vitals are telling us we need to act today.
PATIENT: well, Alright alright And I'll restart that once things calm down right twenty five milligrams like I was taking
PHYSICIAN: Absolutely We'll make sure they give you those instructions and you'll follow up with me next week once you're feeling more stable

NURSE: Alright Oliver, come on in and have a seat. So I've got your chart here and I'm seeing note from last month that we were concerned about some swelling in your legs and also catching you short of breath pretty easy. How are things going since then?
PATIENT: yeah, well, the leg swelling—that's actually gotten a little better, you know? not as puffy as it was. but um, the breathing thing, that's actually worse. like, i woke up this morning and i just couldn't, couldn't catch my breath. even just getting out of bed and walking to the kitchen felt like i'd run a marathon or something.
NURSE: you know, Okay, that's shortness of breath starting this morning and it's been getting worse throughout the day. That concerns me a bit. Have you had chest pain or pressure at all?
PATIENT: No, no chest pain. Just this heaviness, you know, when I try to do anything. And I'm exhausted all the time. Like I sleep eight hours and I wake up I'm already tired. fatigue is just, um, it's really bothersome.
NURSE: um, The fatigue being there alongside the breathing troubles—that's something we need to look at Now I want to ask you your medications Are you taking everything we prescribed I see here you're supposed to be on metformin for your blood sugar
PATIENT: Oh the metforman—yeah I stopped taking that about two weeks ago I mean the eight hundred fifty milligrams pills they were giving me um stomach problems And honestly I just I forgot about it after a while you know how is
NURSE: I understand, but we really need that working for you. What about your montelukast? Are you keeping up with that one?
PATIENT: you know, the montelukast? no, i—wait, no, i stopped that too. that's the one i take once a right? the ten milligrams? i ran out and just never got it refilled. plus with everything going on i just didn't think about it.
NURSE: so, Both of those are important, Oliver. The montelukast helps with inflammation and your breathing, so that's relevant right now. So here's what I'm thinking—given that you're having this severe shortness of breath that started this morning it's worsening, and you've got the fatigue, I want to rule some things out. I'm concerned we might be dealing with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, or we need to at least check that possibility.
PATIENT: heart failure? like my heart's failing? that sounds... that sounds pretty serious. i mean, my neighbor's got gallstones and she's always complaining about stomach pain, but heart stuff—that's different, right?
NURSE: so, It can be serious yes But we're not confirming anything yet—we're just being thorough That's why I want to get some bloodwork done right away and we need to schedule a follow-up visit for you in about a week so we can look at those results and talk about your medications getting back on track
PATIENT: Okay okay so bloodwork What are you looking for in there And um a follow-up visit next week you mean
NURSE: we'll check b-type natriuretic peptide, which tells us about heart stress, your kidney function since you need that metformin too work properly, and your electrolytes. and yes, i want to see you back in about seven days, maybe sooner if your breathing gets any worse. if it gets really bad tonight or you develop pain, you go to the emergency room, okay?
PATIENT: um, Yeah, got it. Go to the ER if it gets really bad. Um, so the gout—I haven't had a flare-up in a few months, is that something I should still be worried about or...?
NURSE: The gout is stable for now, which is good. But let's focus on this breathing issue first. Once we get your restarted—especially the montelukast at ten milligrams daily—and get those labs back, we'll have a clearer picture of whether we're dealing with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction or something else that's treatable.
PATIENT: Alright, so I need to get the bloodwork done... exactly? Today?
NURSE: um, Yes today before you leave We've got a lab tech just down the hall And I'm going to get you refills on both the metforman at eight hundred fifty milligrams twice a day and restart the montelukast—ten milligrams once daily Can you commit to taking those
PATIENT: uh, Yeah, I'll do it. I here you—I know I messed up letting things slide. I'll take them. And the follow-up visit, did you say next week?
NURSE: um, that's right. we'll get you scheduled for seven days from now, and you'll have your bloodwork results by then too. sound good?
PATIENT: yeah, that sounds good. thank you.

PHYSICIAN: um, Hey come in. How've you been since we last saw you a few weeks ago?
PATIENT: Oh, you know, not bad overall, but I've had this cough that started up on Monday. It's kind of a slight thing, but it's getting worse, actually. Like, day by day it's a bit more annoying.
PHYSICIAN: A cough that's worsening since Monday — okay. Any fever, or is it pretty much just a dry thing?
PATIENT: No fever that I've noticed Um it's not like a huge production or anything just kind of there when I breathe Oh and now that you mention it I've been a little short of breath too over the past few days Nothing crazy but I definitely notice it more than usual
PHYSICIAN: you know, Shortness of breath four a few days — got it Any chest pain along with that or are you good their
PATIENT: No, no chest pain. Thank goodness, right? I mean, that's one thing I haven't had to worry about. My chest feels fine, no pressure or anything like that.
PHYSICIAN: well, good, that's reassuring. now, let's talk about your obstructive sleep apnea — how are you managing with that overall? are you using your cpap machine?
PATIENT: you know, yeah, yeah, i try to use it most nights. some nights i miss you know, if i'm going to bed late or whatever, but generally i'm pretty consistent with it. it's helped, i think. at least i'm not as tired during the day.
PHYSICIAN: That's good Let me just check your oxygen saturation real quick with real quick with the pulse ox here
PATIENT: well, go ahead So um I also wanted to ask you — I've been a little forgetful about my medications I know I'm supposed to take the sertralene every day but honestly I can't remember if I'm taking it exactly once a day or I mean I take it but I might skip a day here or there It's the one hundred milligrams one right
PHYSICIAN: yes sertraline one hundred milligrams once daily it's important to keep it consistent if you can even if you occasionally miss a dose let's aim for every single day if possible good news is your is ninety four percent which is stable now what about the pioglitazone — are you still taking that for your diabetes management
PATIENT: oh, uh, the pioglitazone? no, i actually stopped taking that a while back. i think it was... wait, maybe six months ago? i kept forgetting about it, and then i thought, well, maybe i didn't need it anymore. was i supposed to keep taking the thirty milligrams?
PHYSICIAN: uh, We should have talked about that before you stopped Let me make a note to revisit your diabetes control with some follow-up bloodwork okay That'll help us see where you're at
PATIENT: I mean, Yeah, okay. Um, so this cough thing — should I be worried? It's still pretty mild, but like I said, it's getting worse each day.
PHYSICIAN: um, the fact that it's worsening is worth keeping an eye on combined with the shortness of breath you mentioned i think we need to get you seen by cardiology too make sure there's nothing going on with your heart and we'll get that bloodwork ordered too to check your sugars and other markers
